title: Truth to power
hookLine: soft words for hard things: in Tilang, Guru Nanak speaks as the Word comes to him, to Lalo by name, and turns wedding words into plain words for killing

lines: A HYMN WITH NO SOFT WORDS.
cards: Official language has a gift for soft words. An incident. Unrest.
A regrettable loss. A difficult period. Each is true enough to say out loud and vague enough that nobody has to picture anything.
Soft words protect someone. The question is who.
Guru Nanak's hymn in Raga Tilang has no soft words in it at all, and it explains why in its very first line, spoken to a friend, Lalo, whom tradition remembers as a carpenter.

teach.h: AS THE WORD COMES, SO I SPEAK.
teach.b: First, the opening, in paraphrase: as the Word of the Master comes to me, so I speak it, Lalo. That's the hymn's whole method. It doesn't polish the Word into something safer.
It says it as it comes. Earlier on this path we heard this line as courage, and later as truth told at the time of truth. Today, listen for its plainness.

teach.h: VE LALO: SAID TO ONE FRIEND.
teach.b: Line after line ends with ve Lalo, O Lalo. Plain speech here isn't a speech to a crowd or a letter to a palace.
It's said to one man, a working man as tradition remembers him, again and again, the way you'd talk to a friend across a table when something terrible has happened. Third, the words it chooses.
This hymn uses wedding words too, and turns them inside out.
The invader comes like a wedding party, but a wedding party of sin. Wedding songs are sung, but they're songs of blood, and blood takes the place of the red powder a bride wears.
Every pretty word you'd use for a celebration is dragged into the light and made to say exactly what happened: a familiar word forced to tell the truth. Fourth, what that asks of us.
Speaking truth to power, here, isn't shouting. It's refusing to blur: saying the thing as it is, to the person in front of you, by name, kindly, without letting the comfortable word cover it.

how: Sikhs sing this Tilang shabad addressed to Bhai Lalo in kirtan, and its opening line about speaking as the Master's Word comes is cited as a model for honest, fearless speech.

o: naming wrongs plainly, without soft words
the idea that the powerful decide what's true
shouting down rulers in a public square

games.q: inside the Tilang hymn — tap the pairs.
p: O Lalo: the friend named line after line
but a wedding party of sin

s: the hymn is addressed to the new rulers
it is spoken to Lalo, a friend, by name, line after line.
the hymn turns wedding words into words for killing
a wedding party of sin; wedding songs that are songs of blood.

games.q: terrible things have happened, and you must describe them. what words do you reach for?
o: soft ones, so no one is upset.
plain ones, as the Word comes, to a friend by name.
games.why: as the Master's Word comes to me, so I speak, Lalo; and the hymn turns wedding words to say exactly what happened.

practice: Think of something you've been describing to yourself in soft words: a fight you keep calling a misunderstanding, a habit you keep calling a phase, a hurt you keep calling nothing.
Find the plain word for it, then shape a single sentence that's both true and kind for the one person it belongs to, and just hold it, noticing that it can be held. If you pray, say Waheguru once.

wordCard.voice: Truth to power. Guru Nanak's Tilang hymn to Lalo: as the Master's Word comes, so I speak, in plain words that turn wedding songs into songs of blood. Today's word.

orig.note: lalo: the friend the Tilang hymn speaks to, remembered in tradition as a carpenter; line after line, ve Lalo.

carryVoice: Your line: speak as it comes. Plain and kind can share one sentence. Onward.

sources.ref: Tilang, Mahala 1, 'jaisee mai aavai khasam kee baanee taisrraa karee giaan ve laalo', Ang 722–723
